pages.text: Invasive green crabs: If you can't beat them, eat them. | National Geographic By Kea Krause Photographs by Brian Skerry Published July 11, 2022 • 12 min read West Bath, Maine — If you close your eyes, a green crab scuttling up your forearm feels more spider than sea creature, its little legs picking their way as if spinning silk. If you open your eyes, you will see the forged work of 200 million years: bumpy carapace, plated apron, calcified pincers. The small crabs are exquisite, seemingly carved from jade. The big ones are monstrous looking. They are nimble and chaotic, and likely under any beach rock in the Gulf of Maine. But here, the European green crab is not native. It is an invader , a species that traveled to the region in the 1800s in the ballast water of trading ships. In the centuries since, the crabs have established a thriving population, feasting on soft-shell clams and blue mussels, overtaking fisheries that have sustained Mainers for centuries. Their monstrous appetites and canny ability to adapt and reproduce have outcompeted any efforts to remove them. Green crabs ( Carcinus maenas ) are an invasive species that first appeared in New England waters in the 1800s, mostly likely arriving in the onboard water of large oceangoing vessels. The species’ population has exploded in recent years due to warming seawater temperatures in the Gulf of Maine. Now, one of the last defenses against these marauding creatures is not to eradicate them, but to eat them . SBICs invest in small businesses in the form of debt and equity. The SBA doesn’t invest directly into small businesses, but it does provide funding to qualified SBICs with expertise in certain sectors or industries. Those SBICs then use their private funds, along with SBA-guaranteed funding, to invest in small businesses. What you can get SBICs invest in small businesses through debt, equity, or a combination of both. Debt is a loan an SBIC gives to a business, which the business must pay back, along with any interest. Equity is a share of ownership an SBIC gets in a business in exchange for providing funding. The country's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said it targeted the US air defence radar facility at al-Riffa air base in Bahrain using six drones. Bahrain's military said its air defence systems intercepted and destroyed the Iranian air attacks "before they could achieve their objectives". It comes after Iran fired drones at Bahrain on Friday, its first attack against Gulf countries since September. The US and Iran are locked in a stand-off over the Strait of Hormuz. About a fifth of the world's gas and oil supply usually flows through it but shipping has been restricted since the outbreak of war in February. Iran insists that it should control the strait and has been attacking what it calls "unauthorised" traffic, while the US military is providing protection for tankers shuttling oil through the strait to keep exports flowing from Gulf Arab states. pages.text: Is Ichthyotitan the largest marine reptile yet known? | National Geographic SCIENCE The 80-foot-long Ichthyotitan was the killer whale of its time Jawbone fossils suggest Ichthyotitan severensis may have been the largest ichthyosaur yet known—and hunted prey much like orca. An illustration of a giant pair of swimming Ichthyotitan severnensis , a marine reptile that paleontologists believe may have been the orca of its day. Illustration By Gabriel Ugueto - Dean Lomax By Riley Black Last updated September 9, 2025 Ichthyotitan severensis was an absolutely immense ichthyosaur . Apex predators, ichthyosaurs were the orcas of their time , stalking the seas more than 201 million years ago, during the Triassic period . Estimated to be more than 80 feet in length, paleontologists believe I chthyotitan could be the largest ichthyosaur ever discovered. Ichthyotitan’ s discovery dates to 2018, when University of Bristol paleontologist Dean Lomax and his team described a piece of ichthyosaur bone that had been found in the United Kingdom. It was so big that it had previously been mistaken for a dinosaur bone. “When we first described the first specimen, I was hopeful more specimens would come to light,” Lomax says. The huge ichthyosaur may have measured more than 80 feet in length. This bivalve fossil was found on the jaw bone. Photograph By Dr.Lomax Bivalve - Dean Lomax He got his wish. No, it's a 'miraculous' new prehistoric reptile Mirasaura grauvogeli had a featherlike crest and a tail like a monkey. “It's been a long time since I've been so blown away by a new fossil discovery.” By Asher Elbein Published July 23, 2025 Some 247 million years ago, a bizarre, six-inch-long reptile crept down a branch, its prehensile tail and feet clutching the bark like a monkey, and its narrow, birdlike face scanning its surroundings. On its back, an overlapping fan of stiff structures likely caught the light, vibrant with color. They looked very much like feathers, but were something entirely different as the reptile wasn’t related to birds or dinosaurs, and it existed a hundred million years before the first dinosaur took wing . Researchers have long believed things like feathers and fur—complex structures which grow out of the skin, and can be used for insulation, sensing surroundings, visual displays and allowing flight—are largely unique to the lineages that gave rise to birds and mammals. But now, a team of paleontologists have discovered a prehistoric reptile with a regal, plume-like crest that is unlike any previously-known integumentary appendage, things like horns, claws, and hair. pages.text: Is This Where Aristotle Taught Alexander the Great? | National Geographic Premium NEWSLETTERS STONES & BONES Is This Where Aristotle Taught Alexander the Great? Historian Sam Dalrymple travels to Greece to meet an archaeologist who made the discovery of a lifetime. In 343 B.C., Philip of Macedon invited Aristotle, the greatest philosopher of his age, to join his court as tutor to his son as head of the Mieza Gymnasium. Aristotle would not have known it then, but his pupil Alexander the Great would go on to remake the world. Artwork by Armet Portanell, Look and Learn/Bridgeman Images By Sam Dalrymple Published October 30, 2026 I’m Sam Dalrymple , a historian and author of Travels of Samwise and Shattered Lands: Five Partitions and the Making of Modern Asia . Today we're diving into the discovery of Aristotle’s gymnasium. And we'll be back next week covering a controversial dinosaur fossil auction. Sign up here to make sure you don't miss it! I set out to meet archaeologist Angeliki Kottaridi in mid-August, as the temperature of the Pierian range had begun to drop, and the first of the wild cyclamen was beginning to blossom across the Greek countryside. Kottaridi is an energetic eccentric, who began her career studying witches in Greek myth and is now the proud owner of several dozen cats. A former assistant to archaeologist Manolis Andronikos, who found Philip of Macedon's tomb in 1977, Kottaridi later led the Greek excavation of Failaka, the most important Hellenistic site in Kuwait. Isaiah Rashad: Tiny Desk Concert August 25, 2026 5:00 AM ET Bobby Carter Credit: NPR Isaiah Rashad put everything into this Tiny Desk. And in the weeks leading up to the show, we came together to define what "everything" meant for this occasion. So much has happened since The Sun's Tirade in 2016, and through the music, Rashad wanted to talk about it all. As a result, the pride of Chattanooga crafts a performance that feels like a debut for longtime fans and newcomers alike. Only on NPR Isaiah Rashad: 'Time's up for being afraid of yourself' Rashad's music comprises just as much blues as hip-hop, and his strength lies in raw vulnerability, which he consistently expresses through honest songwriting. Album titles like The House is Burning and the latest, IT'S BEEN AWFUL , spell it out plainly: He's going through it. Family, addiction, sexuality — no stone is unturned. Without studio effects, these Tiny Desk arrangements illuminate his melodic foundation and what he calls " rapping in hieroglyphics ," as he told NPR's Rodney Carmichael. With bashful charm, the TDE veteran gives an ambitious, spiritually bookended 13-song set of his best work thus far. Samir Abu Younis, the newly appointed commander of the Rafah Brigade, was killed on Saturday in Al-Mawasi in the southern Gaza Strip, according to Hamas's Al-Qassam Brigades military wing. A local Hamas official confirmed Younis's death. The Israeli military said it had targeted him and that prior to the strike "steps were taken to mitigate harm to civilians". Eyewitnesses in Gaza said four missiles struck a tent in the Al-Waha camp, which shelters hundreds of displaced people in Al-Mawasi, causing a fire to break out. A medical source at Nasser Hospital in the southern city of Khan Younis said three injured people had arrived there, as well as a dead body. The Israel Defence Forces (IDF) and Israel's security agency, the ISA, confirmed in a statement on Telegram that it had "eliminated" Younis. Describing him as a "central figure among Hamas's senior figures", it said he had "acted with the aim of trying to restore the strength of the brigade and the Hamas terrorist organisation". In Monarchs , photographer Jaime Rojo brings together two decades of stunning images documenting one of nature’s most extraordinary migrations, from the forests of Mexico to the fields of the American Midwest, revealing the beauty, chaos, and wonder of these remarkable butterflies. By Alexa Robles-Gil Photographs by Jaime Rojo Published October 16, 2026 In February 2004, Jaime Rojo , a young Spanish photographer, was walking uphill in Sierra Chincua, a forested mountain range in Mexico that doubles as a sanctuary for the tens of millions of monarch butterflies that migrate there each winter. As he climbed with the friends who had brought him, he began to spot monarchs along the path. Only a few at first. But the higher he went, the more he heard a sound in the background, like something whispering in the trees. Suddenly, a swarm of butterflies was flying overhead, millions of orange and black wings fluttering against the blue sky beyond. “There were so many that you could feel a slight breeze when they flew over you,” he says. Peter Van Breukelen/Redferns/Redferns hide caption toggle caption i Peter Van Breukelen/Redferns/Redferns Jack DeJohnette , one of the most daring and dynamic jazz drummers of the last 60 years, with a loose-limbed yet exacting beat that propelled a limitless range of adventurous music, died on Sunday at HealthAlliance Hospital in Kingston, N.Y. He was 83. The cause was congestive heart failure, Lydia DeJohnette, his wife and manager, tells NPR. DeJohnette had a singular voice at the drums: earthy and elastic, instantly recognizable. Rather than focus the articulation of tempo on his ride cymbal, he often distributed his emphasis around the drum set. He adapted this flowing approach from modern jazz innovators like Roy Haynes as well as avant-garde pioneers like Rashied Ali , devising what he called a multidirectional style. pages.text: James Botham: Wales' unlikely hero in historic win over New Zealand - BBC Sport Image source, Huw Evans Picture Agency Image caption, James Botham was man of the match in Wales' historic win over New Zealand By Gareth Rhys Owen BBC Sport Wales Published 16 November 2026 James Botham lay sprawled on the Principality Stadium turf, pain and exhaustion etched across his face. Whenever the whistle blew, the Wales flanker in the red scrum cap took an age to rise. Precious seconds to recover. Nobody counts tackles when the ball is dead. But when play resumed, he was everywhere. Tackling, scrambling, hitting the deck and springing back up. By the final whistle, Botham had helped Wales beat New Zealand for the first time in 73 years. He was man of the match. And as the celebrations began, the tears flowed. Quite an afternoon for a player accustomed to working away from the spotlight. Keeping a Botham out of the headlines was always going to be difficult. His grandfather, Lord Ian Botham , is one of Britain's great sporting celebrities. DeWitt characterized people of Japanese ancestry during World War II. Each morning, I looked forward to discovering and mapping an area adjacent to a one I did the day before. This diary entry serves as an introduction to a series of texts covering the challenges I encountered and how I overcame them. I have also added a “before and after” map excerpt, as well as a short video, to illustrate how my work gradually took shape over time. The Place The Icefields Parkway (Highway 93N), in Alberta, owes its name to the spectacular icefields and glaciers that line the road. The parkway, which is a 232 km stretch of highway cutting through Banff and Jasper National Parks, attracts between 1.2 million and 2 million visitors per year. This weekend, I was at State of the Map 2026, the international OpenStreetMap conference, which took place in Paris this year. Here’s a brief, personal feedback and a round-up of a few presentations that stood out for me. You can also find all the videos at https://peertube.openstreetmap.fr . NB: there is a French version here . This one was translated with the help of DeepL translate. The most inspiring: cartes.app Inspiring: cartes.app is a slightly mad project aimed at creating a new Google Maps, but without its car-centric bias. It started with a single contributor, but he’s managed to build a strong team around him: he has the insight to use the best open-source software components for his project – MapLibre for map navigation, vector tiles for map rendering, Photon for geocoding, and Transitious for public transport. Today, the developer is no longer working alone: he is securing funding and attracting contributors from around the world to improve his app and translate it so it can reach a global audience. It’s a wonderful project worth supporting, and you can do so by subscribing to cartes.app premium for just €1 a month. Jungle: Tiny Desk Concert November 2, 2026 5:00 AM ET Robin Hilton Credit: Photo: Lexy Beale/NPR It's hard for any band to make the old sound completely new, but Jungle has spent much of the past decade transforming vintage soul and R&B into something almost alien. The grooves are deep and warmly familiar, with wistful reflections on love and longing. But even in the brightest moments, there's often a thread of mystery and melancholy that leaves you questioning whether everything is as it seems. Fronted by the trio of Tom McFarland, Josh Lloyd-Watson and Lydia Kitto, Jungle is known for fluid live sets, with songs that spill into each other. True to form, at the Tiny Desk, they perform more than a half-dozen tracks that run together in a single, continuous groove. "We're gonna keep the music rolling," Lloyd-Watson tells the NPR crowd as the band melts seamlessly from 2018's "Beat 54 (All Good Now)" into "Dominoes" from the 2023 album Volcano. pages.text: Jurassic period information and facts | National Geographic SCIENCE What is the Jurassic period and why did it end? The heyday of dinosaurs, the Jurassic era saw Earth’s climate change from hot and dry to humid and subtropical. The Jurassic period was characterized by a warm, wet climate that gave rise to lush vegetation and abundant life. Many new dinosaurs emerged—in great numbers. Above, Dimorphodon reptiles fly over a herd of Mamenchisaurus dinosaurs coming down to a river for a drink. Illustration by CoreyFord, Getty Images By National Geographic Staff Last updated August 18, 2025 The Jurassic is a geologic period that took place about 201.3 million years to 145 million years ago and constitutes the middle part of the Mesozoic era . The Jurassic period was named after the Jura limestone deposits in the Jura Mountains, discovered by German geologist Alexander von Humboldt . Building on this find, French scientist Alexandre Brongniart later coined the Jurassic period. There are three Jurassic time periods: early, middle, and late. Overall, the Jurassic gives us a particularly well-preserved fossil record of prehistoric life, which included theropod dinosaurs that scientists believe evolved to become birds . Thanks to this rich record, we know that the Jurassic was the age of dinosaurs roaming a tropical Earth filled with ferns, flowering plants, and conifers. It was also a time when sea monsters, sharks, and blood-red plankton filled inland seas borne of crumbling landmasses. Here’s what the Jurassic period was really like. Justin Bis Justin Bis is the Chief of Staff for the Office of Technology Commercialization (OTC) at the U.S. Department of Energy (DOE). In this role, he works alongside OTC leadership to maximize the impact of DOE’s investments in technology commercialization, strengthen coordination across the agency, and ensure long-term success. Mr. Bis has more than a decade of experience in government service and public life. He previously served at the White House as Special Assistant to President Trump and Deputy Director of the Presidential Personnel Office, where he managed the appointment of senior government officials responsible for regulating the U.S. financial and energy markets. At DOE, he was the Director of Intergovernmental and External Affairs under Secretary Dan Brouillette, serving as the department’s primary liaison to trade associations, labor unions, and state, local, and tribal governments. Beyond his federal service, Mr. Bis was the Executive Director of the Ohio Republican Party and Ohio Deputy State Director for the Donald J. Trump for President campaign. He holds a Bachelor of Arts in Political Science from Northern Michigan University.

There are more miles of singletrack, more places to camp and dedicated space for races and other large events, all part of a broader effort by the Bureau of Land Management and community partners to keep pace with one of western Colorado’s busiest recreation areas. This fall, the final trail in the North Fruita Desert Trails Master Plan is complete. K2-Play winds for about three miles along the base of the Book Cliffs and completes the final phase of a roughly 30-mile expansion of the 18 Road trail system. Its completion caps years of planning and construction involving the BLM Grand Junction Field Office, Colorado Plateau Mountain Bike Trail Association, Mesa County, City of Fruita, local businesses, professional trail builders and volunteers. pages.text: Khawaja book: Sandpapergate a stench Cricket Australia cannot shake - BBC Sport Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Pat Cummins has led Australia in 43 Tests since 2021 By Stephan Shemilt Cricket Correspondent Published 10 November 2026 There are stories that can damage reputations, tarnish legacies and put asterisks next to achievements. Never-ending sagas, claim and counterclaim, one word against another. Are Pep Guardiola's trophies at Manchester City rendered worthless by financial rule breaches? Would either of the Houston Astros or Boston Red Sox have won the World Series without sign stealing? How much fake blood was spilled by Harlequins? Now, sandpapergate has morphed into Usman Khawaja's-book-gate, opening old wounds and asking questions that have hung over Australian cricket since Cameron Bancroft hid some DIY equipment in his jockstrap in 2018. Published on Tuesday, Khawaja's autobiography – Sabr – is only suggesting what plenty have suspected for the past eight years. It always seemed likely that Bancroft, Steve Smith and David Warner were not the only three members of the Australia camp with knowledge of the sandpaper plot. Careful with his words, perhaps for legal reasons, Khawaja has said enough to reignite a row that once consumed the entire nation of Australia. Crucially, the former batter has not named individuals and, in the opinion of Cricket Australia (CA), not presented enough evidence to merit a new investigation. The battle raged on for three years. By the time the conflict came to a close in 1953, more than 50,000 American soldiers had lost their lives. Kristen Ellis Associate Principal Deputy Under Secretary for the Office of the Under Secretary for Science Kristen Ellis currently serves as the Associate Principal Deputy Under Secretary for the Office of the Under Secretary for Science at the US Department of Energy. This office leads the Genesis Mission on behalf of the Federal government; a majority of DOE’s research portfolio; direct management of 10 of the Department’s national labs and multiple user facilities; and technology commercialization activities. Most recently, she served as Associate Principal Deputy Assistant Secretary for the Office of Regulatory and Policy Affairs within the US Department of Energy’s Environmental Management (EM) Office with a portfolio that included infrastructure disposition, subsurface closure, regulatory compliance, waste and materials management and packaging and transportation. Previously, she was the Director for Regulatory, Intergovernmental, and Stakeholder Engagement within EM, leading regulatory relationships, stakeholder and intergovernmental engagement. She has previously served as EM’s Senior Advisor for STEM and Talent Acquisition, assessing future STEM workforce needs. She led the DOE Office of Public affairs during a presidential transition
